newsitem.title: INDIA: India wheat put under RBI selective credit control.
newsitem.headline: India wheat put under RBI selective credit control.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Tuesday put wheat back under selective credit control for a period of three months, in response to recent price-output developments, the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported.
The minimum margins and level of credit ceiling on advances against wheat stocks for mills and processing units would be 45 percent, the news agency said.
For others, like traders, it would be 60 per cent, and against warehouse receipts would be 45 per cent.

The PTI reported that the RBI said all other stipulations, which were in force prior to the removal of selective credit controls on advances against wheat on October 12, 1993, would now be brought back into force.
The RBI in Bombay was closed on Tuesday for a holiday in the western state of Mahahrastra.
Indian government ministers early this month agreed to pay a bonus of 600 rupees ($16.70) per tonne to farmers in addition to the current purchase price of 4,150 rupees.
The bonus will be payable on wheat offered for sale to procurement agencies for the central pool up to June 10, 1997.

Farmers in the states of Punjab and Haryana, which contribute 80 percent of the country's wheat output, have been agitating for higher prices, seeking parity with the prices at which the government imports wheat.
Bhupinder Singh Mann the president of the farmers organisation Bharatiya Kisan Union (BKU), said the government was paying $180 a tonne for imported wheat.
